title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
authors: Alec Radford, Jong Wook Kim, Chris Hallacy, Aditya Ramesh, Gabriel Goh, Sandhini Agarwal, Girish Sastry, Amanda Askell, Pamela Mishkin, Jack Clark, Gretchen Krueger, Ilya Sutskever

code.title: openai/CLIP
code.note: the released model code and weights (repo, about 15 minutes for the README and the entry path); the training code and the WIT dataset were not released

takeaway: Contrastive pretraining on 400M web image-text pairs yields a shared embedding space where text builds zero-shot classifiers, matching supervised ResNet-50 on ImageNet with far better distribution-shift robustness.
verdict: Believe the method and the headline numbers: they come from released models that later work has re-run widely, and open reproductions matched them. Read "contrastive is 4x more efficient than predicting the words" and "robust because zero-shot" as findings at the paper's scale and on its data: later work traced the robustness mainly to the diversity of the training data, and found captioning competitive for learning representations once data and compute are matched.

headline.d: the original supervised ResNet-50's level; 11.5% for Visual N-Grams

headline.u: faster to the same zero-shot accuracy
headline.k: matching pairs instead of predicting the caption's words
headline.d: and 3x more from bag of words over a captioning Transformer: about 12x in all, at one ResNet-50 scale

headline.k: zero-shot CLIP, against 2.7% for a ResNet-101
headline.d: both score 76.2% on ImageNet; the gap to the shifted sets shrinks by up to 75%

resources.n: the authors' condensed account, with the zero-shot classifier construction shown visually.
places CLIP's loss in the InfoNCE family and derives the surrounding contrastive-learning theory.
CLIP as the foundation of the modern vision-language stack, with a clear walkthrough of the training objective and what came after.
the open reproduction (repo, about 20 minutes for the README and the entry path); the fastest way to read a working implementation and see how the recipe scales on LAION-scale data.

resources.t: Data Determines Distributional Robustness in CLIP
resources.n: the controlled follow-up on section 3.3: of five candidate causes, the diversity of the training distribution explains the robustness; language supervision and the contrastive loss contribute little.

resources.t: Sigmoid Loss for Language Image Pre-Training (SigLIP)
resources.n: the loss most open vision towers now use: each pair is a separate yes or no, so the batch no longer has to be normalised as a whole.

kb.n: 2020: supplies CLIP's best image encoder; CLIP is the main route by which ViT reached multimodal models.
2020: the zero-shot task transfer and prompt engineering CLIP imports into vision, and the WebText-style data behind WIT.

kb.t: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
kb.n: 2020: CLIP's zero-shot error follows the same kind of smooth log-log trend in compute.

kb.t: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models (Stable Diffusion)
kb.n: 2021: conditions image generation on CLIP text-encoder outputs through cross-attention.
2017: both of CLIP's encoders are Transformers (the image one in its ViT variants).
2020: the diffusion line that DALL-E 2 (unCLIP) later conditioned on CLIP image embeddings.

topics.n: vision-language models, vision towers and text-conditioned generation, all built on CLIP-style embeddings.
contrastive learning, the InfoNCE loss and linear probes.
WIT's query-balanced collection, and CLIP-score filtering (LAION, DataComp, DFN).
